pr_title: Throttle scrollbar updates in TermControl to ~one per 8ms
pr_body:
<!-- Enter a brief description/summary of your PR here. What does it fix/what does it change/how was it tested (even manually, if necessary)? -->
## Summary of the Pull Request

Redo #3531 but without the bug that it caused (#3622) which is why it was reverted.

I'm sorry if I explain this badly. If you don't understand a part, make sure to let me know and I will explain it better.

<!-- Other than the issue solved, is this relevant to any other issues/existing PRs? --> 
## References

### Will this reintroduce a crash?

I don't really understand that second check:
https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/pull/3256/files#diff-37b8cdfbaef0c1f807e324f0e6efb4edR1387-R1393
For now I removed it because it seems useless to me and it would make the code more complex.

Indeed, the scroll bar is held by the `TermControl` so if even if `_closing` is `true`, it should still be alive if `this` is alive. And if `this` is not alive, well referencing `_closing` will crash so that check doesn't do better here. So what is it for?

I cannot reproduce the crash from the issue that that PR fixed (#2248). I think that this is thanks to the `weakThis` check (when I remove it, it crashes). So I assume it's fine.

But I need help to know if I should add it back. @mcpiroman what do you think? Do you know if that check actually was useful or if can I remove it?

I'm leaving it as a draft PR until I solve this.

**EDIT:** see discussion below.

* [x] CLA signed. If not, go over [here](https://cla.opensource.microsoft.com/microsoft/Terminal) and sign the CLA
* [ ] Tests added/passed

<!-- Provide a more detailed description of the PR, other things fixed or any additional comments/features here -->
## Detailed Description of the Pull Request / Additional comments

### Explanation

How it worked before:
`Terminal` signals that viewport changed -> `TermControl::_TerminalScrollPositionChanged` gets called on the terminal thread -> it dispatches work for later to be ran the UI thread to updates the scrollbar's values

Why it's bad:
* If we have many viewport changes, it will create a long stack of operations to run. Instead, we should just update the scroll bar with the most recent information that we know.
* Imagine if the rate that the work gets pushed on the UI thread is greater than the rate that it can handle: it might freeze?
* No need to be real time, we can wait just a little bit (8ms) to accumulate viewport changes before we actually change the scroll bar's value because it appears to be expensive (see perf below).

Now:
`Terminal` signals that viewport changed -> `TermControl::_TerminalScrollPositionChanged` gets called on the terminal thread -> it tells the `ScrollBarUpdater` about a new update -> the `ScrollBarUpdater` only runs one job (I don't know if that's the right term) on the UI thread at a time. If a job is already running but hasn't updated the scroll bar yet, it changes the setting in the already existing job to update the scroll bar with the new values. A job "waits" some time before doing the update to throttle updates because we don't need real time scroll bar updates. -> eventually, it updates the scroll bar
If the user scrolls when a scroll bar update is pending, we keep the scroll bar's Maximum and Minimum but let the user choose its new Value with the `CancelPendingValueChange` method.

### Note

Also I changed a little bit the code from the Terminal to notify the TermControl less often when possible (686a7b362ccf2761c9531600c356317a625d9794). I can remove that commit if this is not in scope of this PR.

### Performance

I'm a noob at using the tools to profile an application. Hopefully this is good enough. Perf in release mode while running `1..2000000` in Powershell during the first 4 seconds, without the last commit (686a7b362ccf2761c9531600c356317a625d9794):

Before:
![before](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/56923875/74609840-4d725b00-50ee-11ea-9e10-ea842fa1d00c.png)

After:
![after](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/56923875/74610071-30d72280-50f0-11ea-9aa8-b84fa446f8f6.png)

<!-- Describe how you validated the behavior. Add automated tests wherever possible, but list manual validation steps taken as well -->
## Validation Steps Performed

I tried to scroll with the scroll bar, with the mouse wheel. I tried to scroll while content is being outputted.

I tried to reproduce the crash from #2248 without success (good).
pr_comments:
Yup, this check WAS actually useful; if I recall correctly, the whole PR was about this check :). From the practical point of view, it very deterministically prevented from crash in specified case (this is, when you quickly open and close a tab, if I'm right). 

However, I was strongly suspicious that there's something more going on and even marked that as a quick and hopefully temporary fix. Now that proper handling of `this` pointer appeared, with weak refs and stuff, it is rather apparent to me that it really resolves the problem (at least, it seems like the only practically possible cause of this issue).

I uphold your point about relative lifetimes and so I strongly believe that this check IS NOT longer useful, at least from crash bewareness point of view, but then only IF the whole reference lifetime trickery is done right. Not saying that is not (haven't checked), just that it is often tricky to get it right, especially with what looks like asynchronous callback.

Thank you for the explanation. I agree with you. I'm wondering why the check worked in the first place though. My understanding is that the crash happened because `_scrollBar` was null, and `_scrollBar` was null because `this` was destroyed. But if `this` was destroyed, then surely `_closing` is no longer valid too. So it should still crash, right? Or maybe `_closing` still happened to read as false because the `TermControl` was destroyed but its memory contents are still there for now? This is a mysterious crash.

Anyway, I think I will mark this as ready for review because I wasn't able to reproduce the crash.

Three things:
1. Maybe the code isn't too good: I don't know if the `ScrollBarUpdater` abstraction is good.
2. Although the CPU usage in `TermControl::_TerminalScrollPositionChanged` is lower than before, I'm not sure about the real effects of this on performance globally. It should be better but I don't know a good way to benchmark this.
3. Additionally, we might want the terminal to only send scroll notifications when `Terminal::Write` is completely done so that when the terminal receives multiple `




` it only sends 1 notification at the end of the processing of all of those `
`.

Note to myself and those who're interested from the future (Hi, people from the future, will we ever have flying cars like those in BTTF?) :

Aside from scroll position, cursor position updating should also probably be throttled (`Terminal::_NotifyTerminalCursorPositionChanged`, to be particular). Considering these 2 problems are very much the same, it is kinda justified to have a `TimeThrottle` class.
Oops, I think I didn't rebase correctly 🤣.

I just noticed that when I rewrote the git history while I was trying to do a rebase, it spammed a bunch of merged PRs on this repository with references from commits. Should I delete my GitHub fork and recreate it and maybe the references will be gone? I didn't expect GitHub to do this. Sorry.
Nah, don't worry about it. Happens. :smile:

IIRC, the trick was that the renderer->NotifyScroll was accumulating the delta into the psrSelectionRects, and that overflow was what caused the original bug. If there's no selection, then there's no selection rects in the renderer to accumulate the delta into.

(variable names might be wrong here)

Ok thank you for explaining.

Do you think it's ok if I remove that test and I instead add a more general test that checks if the scrolling is done correctly, but that no longer checks if the selection and renderer behavior works correctly (see 1508ff1895f94373f22b609a4ee5793f30c47dee)?

Here's why I personally think that it's better: instead of mocking the renderer to check if it received the right values, the test was relying on the fact that the function `_NotifyScrollEvent` was always called right after it sent the scroll delta to the renderer. So the test was relying on an implementation detail, and not actually checking if anything overflows (at least this is what I understand, I may be wrong).

The problem is that because I've changed some code, the assumption that the tests relied on is no longer valid so if I want to keep the test I probably have to refactor it and mock things and I don't think that it's worth it.

If you can make a test that can catch the original bug in #5630, then I don't really care if you get rid of the test I added. I just want to make sure that case is caught one way or another, since that was a particularly sneaky bug.

Fortunately, the important part of the bugfix in that issue was [pretty trivial](https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/pull/5630/files#diff-57db0f4e0f835cad32ceff3c30f8a127), so it shouldn't be to hard to revert that section and make sure the new test catches it.

The test I wrote was pretty janky IMO, so I'm happy if it can be replaced with something more... robust 😉 

<hr>

There also may or may not be an aggressive memory leak that this PR fixes. @miniksa and @lhecker are investigating this currently, but our psychic debugging is thinking that this PR will at least improve this scenario

Thanks for this PR! It actually solves half of the problem already. 🙂 (Namely the slowdown, but unfortunately not an associated memory leak of sorts.)

I humbly believe though, that this PR could achieve almost the same effect/improvement, while being simpler in its implementation. What do you think about the following approach @greg904? https://github.com/lhecker/terminal/compare/master...throttle-scrollbar-updates
In my tests it works reasonably well...

Potentially someone could make it even better by abstracting away this entire issue into a `ValueThrottler` or similar. That struct would only need a single method "throttle" and could contain the entire emplace -> sleep -> take cycle, while being generic over T.
@lhecker Yes that's what I was looking for! We are programmers. We don't just make breakfast. We first make a base class called `class Meal` and make `class Breakfast extends Meal`.

Yes. I agree that your code is better. I will modify my PR.

Note that it is missing 2 things that I wanted to add:
* If the user scrolls while we are waiting to update the scrollbar, the user takes priority and it cancels the update
* The first scroll bar update is instant, only the subsequent updates are throttled

These things are probably not very important because the throttle delay is so small though. I will try to find a better abstraction to include them.
Ok, I refactored the code a little bit. I think it's better now. @lhecker what do you think?

The new scroll test catches bug #5540.

**EDIT:** it crashes when resizing the terminal in release mode :(
**EDIT 2:** I fixed it (in bbf6978) by not using coroutines and instead using Dispatcher.RunAsync but I still don't understand where the crash came from. There's a lot of things going on at the same time (lambda with capture, coroutines, weak pointers) so it's a bit hard to understand the flow of the code.

>  don't quite understand the reason behind some of the changes yet (haven't read the linked issues yet 🙈), so the reason for the changes to fakeScroll elude me. Are they necessary to fulfill the title "Throttle scroll position update"? I suppose they are...

This change is not necessary.
While debugging, I found that when new text appears and the buffer is cycled, the terminal still sends a notification to update the scroll bar, even though it is useless because when the buffer is cycled, the scroll bar is already at its maximum and doesn't change. So I added a check to remove this in this PR as well.
But while doing this, I wanted to rename the variable `newRows` to `fakeScroll` and remove the `notifyScroll` variable because I thought it made the code a little less confusing. It is true that this is an unnecessary change. Should I remove it?

I personally feel like the previous code with `newRows` is easier to understand than `fakeScroll`.
The remaining changes (e.g. like `updatedViewport` or renamings like `proposedCursorPosition`) are fine for me. But don't just rely on my opinion - that's up to the maintainers. 😅

I checked this PR out locally and I tested two things:
* Functionality of manual scrolling while an application is printing newlines (aka: `while true; date --rfc-3339=ns; sleep 0.1; end`)
* Performance if an application prints faster than the terminal can process (using `yes` in WSL, then pressing Ctrl+C and measuring how long it takes for the terminal to be responsive again)

The former works just like before and latter is \_vastly\_ improved. I'm giving this PR a big 👍.

---

On another note - and this really is entirely offtopic - I just noticed I'm kinda dissatisfied with the "manual scrolling, while an application is printing newlines" UX. Basically you can scroll upwards right now, but if an application prints a newline your view doesn't stay in place and instead seemingly scrolls down by a line. UX-wise I'm giving that a bit of a 👎. 😄
I think I'll probably propose to change that (i.e. "make scrolling in WT behave like the Gnome/macOS terminals") soonish if no one has done so far.

> Performance if an application prints faster than the terminal can process (using yes in WSL, then pressing Ctrl+C and measuring how long it takes for the terminal to be responsive again

What about in a remote host? I could do a cat on a really long file by mistake (intending to use grep) and when I press ^C, it will either eat it and not care (in that case sometimes ^Z works, sometimes the terminal just becomes completely unresponsive) or it will take a long time for ^C to work.
Thank you so much, @greg904 and @lhecker

issue_context.title: Throttle scrollbar updates to improve performance
issue_context.body:
PR #3531 added this code to throttle scrollbar updates to reduce CPU usage:

https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/blob/ee087cfd2929c1d592e8d169d609da97363d74e7/src/cascadia/TerminalControl/TermControl.cpp#L1419-L1432

But the code skips the last scroll update. If we have 4 updates very quickly, then:
- 1st will set the `_lastScrollTime` and update the scrollbar
- 2nd will return because the time difference is too small but will reset `_lastScrollTime` for the next one (BTW why reset? we could skip the next one too)
- 3rd will set the `_lastScrollTime` and update the scrollbar
- 4th will return because the time difference is too small but will reset `_lastScrollTime` for the next one

So we missed the last update (the 4th) and now the scrollbar has invalid value.

@skyline75489
comments: @greg904 you want to take a crack at this? :smile:

Thanks @greg904 . Is this a theoritical bug or a pratical one that you experienced yourself ? I can't reproduce this kind of inconsistency. Guess most of the time there'll be a fifth update that corrects the state.

And about resetting the value to `nullopt`. I originally put it there to prevent some kind of bad situation. But you're right. It can be safely removed now, I think.

Here is a repro:
1. open terminal with powershell
2. type `1..100`
3. grab scrollbar and scroll a little bit up and then back to the bottom in one go
4. notice that the viewport isn't exactly at the bottom (it is one line above so you don't see the prompt) because the scrollbar's max value hasn't changed so it still thinks that the bottom is the old bottom

@DHowett-MSFT I will try to do a PR but I was waiting for my other PR #3344 to be merged. Or maybe I can also add a fix for this in it?
Let's make sure that 3344 gets reviewed. Really sorry about the delay there. If you want to stage another PR that builds on top of that one, I'm sure that'd be fine :smile:
With #3660 reverting this for v0.7, this is now the "Throttle scrollbar updates to improve perf" issue
